tracks.title: TypeScript
tracks.description: Master the type system: from inference and narrowing to conditional types, variance and senior-level type puzzles.

units.title: Shaping Types
units.description: Interfaces, generics, keyof and indexed access

units.title: Patterns & Ecosystem
units.description: Template literals, unions, strictness, React and Node

units.title: Expert Type Systems
units.description: Variance, brands, recursion and hard puzzles

steps.title: Annotations vs inference
steps.body: TypeScript infers types from initialisers, so you rarely annotate local variables. `const` infers the *literal* type (`"hi"`), while `let` widens to the base type (`string`). Annotate function parameters and public API return types; let inference handle the rest.
steps.code:
const a = "hi";      // type "hi"
let b = "hi";        // type string
const arr = [1, 2];  // number[]
const t = [1, "a"] as const; // readonly [1, "a"]

steps.question: What is the inferred type of `x`?
steps.explanation: A `const` declaration of a string literal gets the literal type `"on"`. With `let` it would widen to `string`.
steps.code: const x = "on";

steps.question: Which statement about `unknown` and `any` is correct?
options: Both let you call any method on the value without checks
`unknown` must be narrowed before use; `any` disables checking
`unknown` is only allowed in strict mode
steps.explanation: `any` opts out of type checking entirely. `unknown` is the type-safe top type: you must narrow it (typeof, instanceof, guards) before using it.

steps.prompt: Fill in the return type that means 'never returns normally' (always throws).
steps.explanation: `never` is the bottom type: no value can be produced, so a function that always throws (or loops forever) returns `never`.

steps.question: Does this compile under `strict`?
steps.explanation: `age` is inferred as `number` from the initialiser, so assigning a string is an error (TS2322).
steps.code:
let age = 30;
age = "thirty";

steps.question: What is the type of `pair`?
steps.explanation: Without an annotation or `as const`, an array literal infers an array of the union of element types, not a tuple.
steps.code: const pair = ["a", 1];

steps.prompt: Arrays and tuples are both plain arrays at runtime. Print `Array.isArray(t)` and then `t.length` on separate lines (types are erased).
steps.starter:
const t = ["a", 1];
// print Array.isArray(t) then t.length

steps.title: Unions and intersections
steps.body: `A | B` means a value is *either* A or B, so you may only use members common to both until you narrow. `A & B` means the value is *both*, so it has all members of each. Intersections of object types merge their properties; intersecting disjoint literal types yields `never`.

steps.question: Which operation is allowed on `v` without narrowing?
steps.explanation: Only members present on every constituent are accessible. `toString` exists on both `string` and `number`; the others exist on only one.
steps.code: declare const v: string | number;

steps.question: What is `("a" | "b") & ("b" | "c")`?
steps.explanation: Intersection distributes over unions: only `"b"` is in both sets.

steps.question: What is the type of `x.name`?
steps.explanation: Intersecting object types combines their members: `x` has both `name` and `age`.

steps.prompt: Complete the type so `Result` is either of two literal types.
steps.code: type Result = "ok" ____ "error";
steps.explanation: `|` builds a union of the two literal types.

steps.question: Why does this fail to compile under `strictNullChecks`?
steps.explanation: `null` is a distinct type; check before dereferencing (`p?.name` or an `if`).

steps.question: Given `type U = string | number | boolean`, what is `Exclude<U, string>`?
steps.explanation: `Exclude<T, U>` removes members of T assignable to U, leaving `number | boolean`.

steps.title: How narrowing works
steps.body: Control-flow analysis narrows a union inside branches. Built-in narrowing constructs: `typeof x === "string"`, `instanceof`, `in`, truthiness, equality (`===`), and discriminant checks. You can add your own with user-defined guards (`x is T`) and assertion functions (`asserts x is T`).

steps.question: Inside the `if`, what is the type of `x`?
steps.explanation: Truthiness excludes `null`. The remaining members are `string | number`.

steps.question: What does the `in` check narrow `a` to?
steps.explanation: `"meow" in a` narrows to the union members that have that property: `Cat`.

steps.title: User-defined type guards
steps.body: A function returning `x is T` tells the compiler that a `true` result narrows the argument. The compiler trusts you: a wrong guard is silent unsoundness. Assertion functions (`asserts x is T`) narrow after the call returns instead of in a branch.

steps.explanation: A type predicate has the form `param is Type`.

steps.question: What is the type of `r`?
steps.explanation: A type-guard callback selects the overload `filter<S extends T>(pred: (v: T) => v is S): S[]`, so the result is `string[]`.
steps.code:
const xs: (string | null)[] = ["a", null];
const r = xs.filter((x): x is string => x !== null);

steps.question: Which input makes this guard lie about its claim?
options: `[1, 2]`, since arrays satisfy `typeof === "object"` but are rarely meant as records
steps.explanation: The guard excludes `null` and primitives, but arrays pass. Type predicates are unchecked assertions, so the body must really verify what the signature promises.

steps.prompt: Runtime gotcha: print `typeof` of each value in `["a", 1, null, [1]]` joined with commas.
steps.starter:
const vals = ["a", 1, null, [1]];
// print typeof of each, joined by ','
steps.solution:
const vals = ["a", 1, null, [1]];
console.log(vals.map(v => typeof v).join(','));

steps.title: Two ways to name an object type
steps.body: `interface` and `type` overlap heavily for object shapes. Differences: interfaces support declaration merging and `extends` (with good error messages); type aliases can also name unions, tuples, primitives, mapped and conditional types. Classes can `implements` either when the type is an object type with statically known members.

steps.question: Which can NOT be expressed directly with `interface`?
steps.explanation: Interfaces describe object-like shapes (including callable and constructable ones). Unions need `type`.

steps.question: What happens with two `interface Config` declarations in the same scope?
steps.explanation: Declaration merging combines members. This is how libraries are augmented (e.g. adding fields to Express's `Request`).

steps.question: Does this compile?
steps.explanation: Fresh object literals undergo excess property checks. Assigning via an intermediate variable would pass, since structural typing allows extra props.
steps.code:
interface P { x: number; y: number }
const p: P = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 };

steps.prompt: Fill in the keyword so `Admin` inherits from `User`.
steps.code:
interface User { id: number }
interface Admin ____ User { role: string }
steps.explanation: `interface Admin extends User` copies members; the equivalent with aliases uses `&`.

steps.question: Which best summarises structural typing?
options: Types are compatible only if declared with the same name
Types are compatible when their shapes are compatible
steps.explanation: TS is structural: a value with the required members is assignable regardless of the declared name. (Private/protected members make classes effectively nominal.)

steps.question: How do you create a union of two interfaces?
steps.explanation: Use a type alias; an interface can only extend object types with statically known members, not a union.

steps.title: Generics
steps.body: Generics parameterise a type over other types. A constraint (`T extends U`) restricts what can be passed, and lets you use U's members inside. Type arguments are normally inferred from call arguments. Defaults (`<T = string>`) fill missing arguments.

steps.question: What is the inferred type of `r`?
steps.explanation: `T` is inferred as `string` from `string[]`; the function returns `T | undefined`.
steps.code:
function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined { return xs[0]; }
const r = first(["a", "b"]);

steps.question: Why is this an error?
options: `T` has no members known inside the body
steps.explanation: An unconstrained `T` could be anything, so `.id` isn't allowed. Add `T extends { id: unknown }`.

steps.question: What type is inferred for `K` in the call?
steps.explanation: A `K extends keyof T` parameter keeps the literal type of the argument, so `K` is `"name"` and the result is `string`.

steps.prompt: Add the constraint so `T` must have a string `id`.
steps.explanation: Constraints use `extends` in type parameter lists.

steps.question: With `function identity<T>(x: T): T`, what is the result type of `identity([1, 2] as const)`?
steps.explanation: `as const` makes the argument `readonly [1, 2]`, and `T` is inferred as exactly that.

steps.question: What is the code smell here?
options: `T` appears only once in the signature, so it relates nothing; use `(xs: string[])`
steps.explanation: A type parameter used only once adds no relationship between inputs and outputs. Prefer the concrete type.
steps.code: function logAll<T extends string[]>(xs: T): void {}

steps.title: Type-level operators
steps.body: `keyof T` is the union of T's property names. `typeof x` in a *type position* gives the type of a value. `T[K]` is an indexed access type. Combine them: `keyof typeof obj`, `(typeof arr)[number]`.

steps.question: What is `keyof { a: 1; b: 2 }`?
steps.explanation: `keyof` yields the union of property-name literals.

steps.question: What is `Role`?
steps.explanation: `as const` makes a readonly tuple of literals; indexing with `number` gives the union of element types.
steps.code:
const roles = ["admin", "user"] as const;
type Role = (typeof roles)[number];

steps.question: What is `keyof { [k: string]: boolean }`?
steps.explanation: A string index signature also accepts numeric keys (`obj[1]` is `obj["1"]`), so `keyof` gives `string | number`.

steps.prompt: Complete the indexed access type for the type of `name`.
steps.code:
type User = { id: number; name: string };
type N = User____;
steps.explanation: `User["name"]` is `string`.

steps.question: What does `typeof` do in `type T = typeof x`?
options: Gets the static type of the value `x`
steps.explanation: In type positions `typeof` is a type query, distinct from the runtime `typeof` operator.

steps.question: What is `ReturnType<typeof f>`?
steps.explanation: `typeof f` is the function type; `ReturnType` extracts its return type `number`.
steps.code: function f() { return 1; }

steps.title: Mapped types
steps.body: A mapped type iterates over a union of keys and builds a new object type: `{ [K in Keys]: ValueType }`. Modifiers `readonly` and `?` can be added or removed with `+`/`-`. Key remapping with `as` lets you rename or filter keys. Homomorphic mapped types (`[K in keyof T]`) preserve modifiers of T.

steps.question: What is `Flags` ?
steps.explanation: The mapped type iterates over `"a" | "b"` and gives every property type `boolean`.
steps.code: type Flags = { [K in "a" | "b"]: boolean };

steps.question: What does `-?` do?
steps.explanation: `-?` strips the optional modifier. In a homomorphic mapped type it also removes the implicit `undefined` that optionality added to the value type.

steps.prompt: Complete the mapped type that makes every property of `T` readonly.
steps.code: type Frozen<T> = { ____ [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
steps.explanation: `readonly` before the key makes the property readonly.

steps.question: What is `Keys`?
steps.explanation: The `as` clause filters keys: for `b` the condition `number extends string` is false, so the key maps to `never` and is dropped. Only `"a"` remains.
steps.code:
type OnlyStr<T> = { [K in keyof T as T[K] extends string ? K : never]: T[K] };
type Keys = keyof OnlyStr<{ a: string; b: number }>;

steps.question: Which is true of homomorphic mapped types over arrays/tuples?
options: `{ [K in keyof T]: X<T[K]> }` with T an array/tuple type produces an array/tuple type
They can't be used with generics
steps.explanation: When T is a generic array or tuple type, a homomorphic mapped type maps the elements and keeps the array/tuple shape.

steps.question: What is `Result`?
options: `{ readonly id: number; readonly name: string }`
steps.explanation: The built-in `Readonly<T>` is `{ readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }`.
steps.code: type Result = Readonly<{ id: number; name: string }>;

steps.title: Conditional types
steps.body: `T extends U ? X : Y` picks a branch based on assignability. When `T` is a *naked* type parameter and instantiated with a union, the conditional **distributes** over the members. `infer` declares a type variable inside the `extends` clause that the compiler solves for.

steps.question: What is `IsString<string | number>`?
steps.explanation: Distribution: `IsString<string> | IsString<number>` = `true | false` = `boolean`.
steps.code: type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;

steps.question: How do you stop distribution?
options: Wrap both sides in tuples: `[T] extends [U] ? ...`
steps.explanation: Distribution only happens for naked type parameters. Wrapping in a tuple makes it non-distributive.

steps.question: What is `ElementOf<string[] | number[]>`?
steps.explanation: `ElementOf` distributes: `string[]` yields `string`, `number[]` yields `number`; the union is `string | number`.
steps.code: type ElementOf<T> = T extends (infer E)[] ? E : never;

steps.prompt: Complete the type that extracts the resolved value of a Promise.
steps.code: type Awaited2<T> = T extends Promise<____ U> ? U : T;
steps.explanation: `infer U` declares U inside the conditional's extends clause.

steps.question: What is `P`?
steps.explanation: `Parameters<T>` is defined as `T extends (...args: infer P) => any ? P : never`, giving the parameter tuple.
steps.code: type P = Parameters<(a: number, b: string) => void>;

steps.question: What is `X`?
steps.explanation: Distribution over the empty union (`never`) yields `never`: a distributive conditional applied to `never` produces `never` without evaluating a branch.
steps.code:
type ToStr<T> = T extends unknown ? string : number;
type X = ToStr<never>;

steps.question: What does this evaluate to?
steps.explanation: Optional property `a?: 1` allows `undefined`, so `{a?: 1}` is not assignable to `{a: 1}`; `{a:1}` is assignable to `{a?:1}` but not vice versa.
steps.code: type R = { a?: 1 } extends { a: 1 } ? "yes" : "no";

steps.title: The utility toolbox
steps.body: `Partial<T>` makes props optional; `Required<T>` the opposite; `Readonly<T>` freezes them. `Pick<T,K>` / `Omit<T,K>` select or drop keys. `Record<K,V>` builds a map type. `Exclude`/`Extract`/`NonNullable` operate on unions. `ReturnType`, `Parameters`, `ConstructorParameters`, `InstanceType`, and `Awaited` extract function/class/promise types.

steps.question: What is `Omit<{a:1;b:2;c:3}, "a" | "b">`?
steps.explanation: `Omit` removes the listed keys, leaving `{ c: 3 }`.

steps.question: What is `Extract<"a" | "b" | 1, string>`?
steps.explanation: `Extract<T, U>` keeps members of T assignable to U.

steps.question: What is `Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>>`?
steps.explanation: `Awaited` recursively unwraps thenables, giving `number`.

steps.prompt: Use a utility type so `patch` accepts any subset of `User`'s fields.
steps.code:
interface User { id: number; name: string }
function update(id: number, patch: ____<User>) {}
steps.explanation: `Partial<User>` makes every property optional.

steps.question: Which statement about `Omit` is true?
options: `Omit<T, K>` requires K to be a key of T
`Omit<T, K>` accepts any string key, including ones not in T
steps.explanation: `Omit<T, K extends keyof any>` does not check K against `keyof T`, so typos are silently accepted. `Pick` does check. Also `Omit` is not distributive and collapses unions of object types.

steps.question: What is `NonNullable<string | null | undefined>`?
steps.explanation: `NonNullable` removes `null` and `undefined`.

steps.question: Which builds `{ [k in 'a'|'b']: number }`?
steps.explanation: `Record<K, V>` maps each key in K to V.

steps.title: Template literal types
steps.body: Template literal types build string types from other types: `` `${A}-${B}` ``. They distribute over unions (cartesian product). Intrinsic helpers `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize`, `Uncapitalize` transform casing. In conditional types you can `infer` pieces of a string pattern to parse it at the type level.

steps.question: How many members does `` `${"a"|"b"}${1|2|3}` `` have?
steps.explanation: The cartesian product has 2 x 3 = 6 members.

steps.question: What is `Capitalize<"hello">`?
steps.explanation: `Capitalize` upper-cases the first character.

steps.question: What is `T`?
steps.explanation: The pattern `hello ${infer R}` matches and R captures the remainder.
steps.code:
type After<S> = S extends `hello ${infer R}` ? R : never;
type T = After<"hello world">;

steps.prompt: Complete the key-remapping so `Events<{click: 1}>` yields `{ onClick: 1 }`.
steps.code: type Events<T> = { [K in keyof T as `on${____<string & K>}`]: T[K] };
steps.explanation: `Capitalize` upper-cases the first letter, giving `onClick`.

steps.question: What does `infer H` capture in `S extends `${infer H}${infer R}``?
options: The first character, with R being the rest
steps.explanation: When two adjacent inferences sit in a template, the first infers a single character and the last takes the rest.

steps.question: What is the downside of heavy template-literal parsing types?
options: Deep recursion can hit the compiler's instantiation depth and slow editors
steps.explanation: Recursive type-level parsing is limited (depth ~50 non-tail, ~1000 for tail-recursive conditionals) and can slow type checking.

steps.title: Discriminated unions
steps.body: Give every variant a literal-typed tag (the discriminant) and the compiler narrows on it. Add an exhaustiveness check by assigning the leftover value to `never`: when you add a variant and forget a case, the assignment fails at compile time.

steps.question: In the `default` branch, what is the type of `s` after handling both cases?
steps.explanation: All members are eliminated, leaving the empty union `never`. That's why `const _x: never = s` works as a check.

steps.question: You add `{ kind: "tri"; ... }` to `Shape` without updating `area`. What happens?
options: A compile error at `const _x: never = s`
steps.explanation: `s` would be the `tri` variant in `default`, not assignable to `never`, so the compiler flags the missing case.

steps.prompt: Complete the helper used for exhaustiveness.
steps.explanation: Typing the parameter as `never` means callers can only pass it when all cases are handled.

steps.question: Which property can serve as a discriminant?
options: A property with a literal type (or `undefined`/`null`) that differs between members
steps.explanation: Discriminants need unit/literal types that are unique per variant so equality checks narrow the union.

steps.question: Does `noImplicitReturns` plus a `switch` over a discriminated union without default still require exhaustiveness?
options: Yes: if the switch is exhaustive, TS knows the end is unreachable and does not complain
steps.explanation: If every case returns, control flow analysis sees the fall-off as unreachable (the switch condition narrows to `never`).

steps.question: What type does `s.r` give outside of narrowing?
options: Compile error: `r` doesn't exist on all members
steps.explanation: Property access on a union requires the property to exist on every member.
steps.code:
declare const s: Shape;
s.r;

steps.title: What `strict` turns on
steps.body: `"strict": true` enables a family of flags: `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks`, `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictBindCallApply`, `strictPropertyInitialization`, `noImplicitThis`, `alwaysStrict`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables`. Common extras that are *not* in strict: `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `noImplicitOverride`.
steps.code:
{ "compilerOptions": { "strict": true,
  "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true } }

steps.question: With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, what is the type of `xs[0]` for `xs: string[]`?
steps.explanation: Indexing may be out of bounds, so the flag adds `undefined` to index results.

steps.question: Under `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, what is `e` in `catch (e)`?
steps.explanation: Catch variables are `unknown`; narrow with `instanceof Error` before using `.message`.

steps.title: .d.ts files
steps.body: Declaration files describe the types of JavaScript code without implementation. `declare` introduces ambient declarations. Libraries ship `.d.ts` via the `types` field, or you install `@types/*` packages from DefinitelyTyped. Module augmentation uses `declare module "x" { ... }` to extend existing typings.

steps.prompt: Complete the ambient declaration for a global variable.
steps.code: ____ const API_URL: string;
steps.explanation: `declare` tells the compiler a value exists at runtime without emitting code.

steps.question: What does `skipLibCheck: true` do?
options: Skips type-checking of all `.d.ts` files, speeding up builds and hiding errors inside library typings
steps.explanation: It skips checking declaration files. It trades safety within library typings for speed and avoids conflicts between library versions.

steps.question: Why might `import x from "./data.json"` fail?
steps.explanation: Importing JSON needs `resolveJsonModule` (and often `esModuleInterop` for default imports).

steps.question: What's the safest way to type an untyped third-party module quickly?
options: `declare module "lib";` (everything becomes `any`) as a stopgap, then add real types
steps.explanation: A shorthand ambient module gives `any`-typed exports with minimal noise; replace it with real declarations or `@types` when possible.

steps.title: Typing React props and hooks
steps.body: Type props with an interface or alias and annotate the function parameter directly. `useState<T>()` infers from the initial value; give an explicit generic when the initial value is `null`. Events are typed by `React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>` etc. Prefer discriminated union props over many optional booleans.

steps.question: Why is `useState<User | null>(null)` needed?
options: Without it the state would be inferred as `null` only
steps.explanation: `useState(null)` infers `null`, so `setUser(user)` would fail. Provide the union explicitly.

steps.question: What is the best typing for a component with mutually exclusive props (`href` XOR `onClick`)?
options: A discriminated or union props type, e.g. `{ href: string; onClick?: never } | { onClick: () => void; href?: never }`
steps.explanation: Unions with `never` on the excluded fields make the invalid combination unrepresentable.

steps.title: Typing Node code
steps.body: Use `@types/node` for core modules. Validate external input (env vars, JSON, request bodies) as `unknown`, then parse into a trusted type; `process.env.X` is `string | undefined`. Express handlers get types via generics: `Request<Params, ResBody, ReqBody, Query>`. Type assertions (`as`) do not validate anything at runtime; use schema validators for boundaries.

steps.question: What is the type of `process.env.PORT`?
steps.explanation: Env variables may be missing, so the type is `string | undefined`.

steps.prompt: Narrow the unknown JSON before use. Fill the operator that checks for an object.
steps.explanation: `typeof` returns `"object"` for objects and `null`, hence the extra null check.

steps.question: Which is true about `const user = JSON.parse(text) as User`?
options: It validates the shape at runtime
It only tells the compiler to trust you; wrong data still flows through
It converts to a class instance
steps.explanation: `as` is a compile-time assertion; runtime validation needs explicit checks or a schema library.

steps.title: Covariance, contravariance, invariance
steps.body: If `Dog extends Animal`: a producer (`() => Dog`) is assignable to `() => Animal` (covariant in the return type). A consumer `(a: Animal) => void` is assignable to `(d: Dog) => void` (contravariant in the parameter) under `strictFunctionTypes`. A type that both reads and writes is invariant in theory, but TS treats arrays and *method-syntax* members bivariantly for pragmatism. Explicit annotations `in`/`out` (TS 4.7) document and verify variance for type parameters.

steps.question: Under `strictFunctionTypes`, is this assignment allowed?
steps.explanation: `(d: Dog) => void` requires a function that accepts Dogs only; assigning it to `(a: Animal) => void` would let callers pass any Animal. Parameters are contravariant, so it's an error.

steps.question: Why does this compile (unsound!) even in strict mode?
steps.explanation: TS treats `Dog[]` as assignable to `Animal[]` even though writes through the alias can break the original array. It's a deliberate unsoundness for usability.

steps.question: Why is `Handler` bivariant in its parameter despite `strictFunctionTypes`?
options: Method shorthand declarations are exempt from strictFunctionTypes
Because the return type is void
steps.explanation: Methods declared with method syntax (`handle(e: X): void`) are compared bivariantly. Property syntax (`handle: (e: X) => void`) is checked contravariantly.
steps.code: interface Handler { handle(e: Dog): void }

steps.prompt: Annotate `T` as covariant (output-only) using the variance modifier.
steps.code: interface Producer<____ T> { get(): T }
steps.explanation: `out T` declares T used only in output positions; TS verifies it.

steps.question: Which interface is invariant in `T`?
options: `interface C<T> { get: () => T; set: (v: T) => void }`
steps.explanation: C both produces and consumes T (with property syntax), so neither direction is safe: invariant. A is covariant, B contravariant, D bivariant/unused.

steps.question: What is the result?
steps.explanation: The conditional `T extends (arg: infer A) => void ? A : never` infers `A` in a contravariant position; with a single candidate the result is `number`. With multiple candidates in that position, inference produces an intersection instead of a union.
steps.code:
type Arg<T> = T extends (a: infer A) => void ? A : never;
type R = Arg<(a: number) => void>;

steps.question: What is `U`?
steps.explanation: Multiple candidates for `infer` in a *contravariant* position are intersected; in covariant positions they are unioned. This is the classic union-to-intersection trick.

steps.title: Reading hard types
steps.body: Work systematically: (1) identify distribution points (naked type params in conditionals), (2) evaluate for each union member, (3) note where `never` collapses, (4) remember that mapped types over `keyof T` are homomorphic. Recursion is allowed in conditional types; tail-recursive forms are optimised.

steps.question: What is `Q`?
steps.explanation: Peel the head, reverse the rest, append head: [3,2] then 1 gives `[3, 2, 1]`.
steps.code:
type Reverse<T extends unknown[]> = T extends [infer H, ...infer R] ? [...Reverse<R>, H] : [];
type Q = Reverse<[1, 2, 3]>;

steps.question: What is `Keys`?
steps.explanation: `RequiredKeys` keeps keys where `{} extends Pick<T,K>` is false, i.e. required ones. `a` is required, `b` is optional.
steps.code:
type RequiredKeys<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: {} extends Pick<T, K> ? never : K }[keyof T];
type Keys = RequiredKeys<{ a: string; b?: number }>;

steps.question: What is `IsNever<never>` with the naive definition?
steps.explanation: A naked `T` in a conditional distributes; over `never` it produces `never`, not `true`. Use `[T] extends [never] ? true : false` to detect never.
steps.code: type IsNever<T> = T extends never ? true : false;

steps.question: What is `Last`?
steps.explanation: The pattern `[...infer _, infer L]` matches a tuple's final element.
steps.code:
type Last<T extends unknown[]> = T extends [...unknown[], infer L] ? L : never;
type R = Last<[1, 2, 3]>;

steps.prompt: Fix the type so that `Len<[1,2,3]>` is `3`. Fill the property.
steps.code: type Len<T extends readonly unknown[]> = T["____"];
steps.explanation: The `length` of a tuple type is a numeric literal type.

steps.question: What does this type compute?
options: Keys of T that are functions
Keys of T that are not functions
Methods of T as a union of their return types
steps.explanation: For each key, map to the key if its value extends a function, otherwise `never`; indexing with `keyof T` gathers the union of surviving keys.
steps.code: type FnKeys<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends (...a: any[]) => any ? K : never }[keyof T];

steps.question: Why does the following call error?
options: `T` is inferred as `string` but the second arg is a number
steps.explanation: Both arguments produce candidates for `T` (`string` and `number`). TypeScript does not widen to a union by itself here: it picks `string` from the first argument, then reports that `number` isn't assignable to it. Use two type parameters or `<T extends unknown>` patterns to allow different types.
steps.code:
declare function same<T>(a: T, b: T): T;
same("a", 1);

steps.title: Nominal-ish typing with brands
steps.body: Because TS is structural, `UserId` and `OrderId` (both `string`) are interchangeable. A *brand* adds a phantom property to make them incompatible. The brand exists only in the type system; construct values through a smart constructor.

steps.question: Does `getUser("abc")` compile when the parameter is `UserId`?
options: Yes, strings are assignable to intersections
steps.explanation: A plain `string` lacks the `__brand` property, so it isn't assignable to `string & { __brand: "UserId" }`.

steps.question: What is the runtime cost of a brand?
options: A property is added to each string
None: it's erased and only affects type-checking
steps.explanation: Brands are phantom types: no runtime representation.

steps.title: Recursive types
steps.body: Types can refer to themselves, enabling JSON types, deep readonly, and path types. Deep mapped types should guard against functions and primitives. Beware very deep recursion: the compiler enforces limits (error TS2589 'excessively deep').

steps.question: What is `DeepReadonly<{a: {b: number}}>`?
steps.explanation: The recursion applies `readonly` at every object level.

steps.prompt: Name the escape hatch: write the TS error-suppression comment that fails if there is NO error on the next line (prefer it to `@ts-ignore`).
steps.code:
// @ts-____
const n: number = "x";
steps.explanation: `@ts-expect-error` errors when the next line has no error, so stale suppressions get flagged.

steps.question: Which is a known soundness hole in TS?
options: Calling a function with wrong argument count
Assigning through a covariant array alias, or trusting `as` assertions and non-null `!`
steps.explanation: Array covariance, method bivariance, user type predicates, `as`/`!` and index signatures without `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` all let unsound code compile.

steps.question: What does `satisfies` do in `const c = { a: 1 } satisfies Record<string, number>`?
options: Checks the value against the type while preserving the narrower inferred type `{ a: number }`
Is identical to a type annotation
steps.explanation: `satisfies` (TS 4.9) validates without widening, so `c.a` is known to exist, unlike with a `Record` annotation.
